channel.title: Daily Recap — 🚀 Space News
channel.description: What happened in 🚀 Space News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Astronomy Picture of the Day: Rosetta's selfie above comet 67P
item.description:
Today's Astronomy Picture of the Day is a selfie with real history behind it. Snapped on October 7, 2014, it shows the Rosetta spacecraft's solar array in the foreground with comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko looming beyond — dust and gas streaming away from its curious double-lobed nucleus, sunlight glinting off a 14-meter solar array.

At the time, Rosetta was about 472 million kilometers from Earth but only 16 kilometers from the comet's surface. The image combined two exposures, one short and one long, taken by the CIVA camera on the still-attached Philae lander — and it was the last image from Philae's camera before the lander separated on November 12 to begin its descent to the comet's nucleus, where its chosen landing site sat on the visible hemisphere of the smaller lobe.

Sources

  • NASA: APOD: 2026 October 24 – Rosetta’s Selfie

item.title: NASA overhauls Artemis lander plans, sets 2028 Moon missions in motion
item.description:
NASA announced a major reshaping of its Artemis lunar program, streamlining the designs and operations of the crewed landers being built by Blue Origin and SpaceX for missions targeted at 2028. The agency says the changes, made with both commercial partners, accelerate lander development as it works toward returning astronauts to the lunar surface and establishing a long-term presence there.

Before any landing attempt, Artemis III will fly in 2027 as a dress rehearsal: astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano will take Orion into low Earth orbit to test future lander operations in one of the most complex test missions in NASA's history. NASA also says it has finally resolved a long-festering Orion issue, removing a lingering obstacle from the program. The message from the agency is confidence — mandate, resources, and stakeholder support are in place — with the next two years now the proving ground for the return to the Moon.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: NASA updates lander plans for Moon landings, finally solves long-festering Orion issue
  • NASA: NASA, Partners Accelerate Lander Development for 2028 Moon Missions
  • NASA: NASA’s Artemis III Mission to Test Future Moon Lander Operations

item.title: NASA's Swift observatory ends its mission after two decades of discovery
item.description:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission, making its final observation on October 20. The spacecraft now orbits less than 171 miles above Earth, where increased atmospheric drag prevents its telescopes from steadily tracking their targets — a natural end for a mission that far outlived its original design life.

Swift leaves behind what NASA calls a scientific bonanza, having spent years chasing gamma-ray bursts and other fleeting cosmic events and alerting observatories around the world to catch them. Its legacy is a vast archive that astronomers will keep mining, and a rapid-response model that reshaped how the field studies the universe's most violent, transient phenomena.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA’s Swift Mission Ends, Leaves Behind Scientific Bonanza

item.title: Space Force hunts for a new spaceport site by 2030
item.description:
Pressure is building inside the Pentagon to find a home for a new Space Force spaceport, with a senior commander saying the service needs one in place by 2030. Existing launch ranges are increasingly congested as both military and commercial launch demand grows, and a dedicated site would give the Space Force more control over its own access to orbit.

Options on the table include a public-private partnership, a federal installation, or state land, each with different trade-offs in cost, control, and speed. Where things stand: the requirement is now public and the clock is set, but no site has been chosen — the coming years will be a contest between states and partners vying to host the military's newest gateway to space.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Inside the Pentagon, the pressure is on to find a home for a new spaceport

item.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX passes on military launches, Spain's rocket nears readiness
item.description:
This week's Rocket Report leads with SpaceX declining military launch work, a notable stance from the company that already dominates the commercial launch market, alongside news that Spain's homegrown rocket is nearly ready for flight. The Spanish effort reflects a broader push in Europe for independent launch capability, echoed by the sentiment that countries like Canada should be able to reach orbit on their own terms.

Why it matters: the launch market is fragmenting as more nations and companies build their own rockets rather than relying on a handful of providers. SpaceX's selective approach to military contracts and Europe's maturing small-launch sector both point to a future where access to orbit is more distributed — and more competitive.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: Rocket Report: SpaceX says no thanks to military launches; Spanish rocket nearly ready

item.title: Artemis Moon landing will take ~22 Starship launches, new estimate says
item.description:
A new estimate puts the number of Starship launches needed to support a crewed Artemis Moon landing at 22 — most of them tanker flights to refuel the lunar lander in orbit. The scale of orbital refueling remains the program's defining challenge: the lander needs numerous fuelings before it's ready to descend.

This is the math that keeps Artemis timelines slipping. Every added refueling flight multiplies launch cadence, pad turnaround, and rendezvous complexity. The architecture can work, but 22 launches for one landing is a logistical mountain — and the estimate is a reminder that the Moon program's bottleneck is fuel logistics, not rockets.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Latest estimate for Starship launches required to support a Moon landing? 22.

item.title: US official says Russia's "stalker" satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon
item.description:
A US official says Russia's so-called "stalker" satellite — which has been shadowing other spacecraft in orbit — sure looks like an orbital weapon. Moscow, through the same official who previously called commercial satellites "legitimate targets," now insists the concerns are "unfounded" and the satellite is purely peaceful.

The exchange captures the current state of space security: maneuvering satellites that could be inspectors or could be weapons, with no way to tell from the outside. With commercial constellations now explicitly named as targets by Russian officials, the diplomatic guardrails in orbit are visibly eroding — and the US is no longer being subtle about saying so.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: US official: Russia's stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon

item.title: SpaceX to attempt Starship booster catch on next flight, targeting weekly launches by early 2027
item.description:
SpaceX is going for the booster catch on Starship's next flight, the next milestone in its quest for a fully reusable super-heavy rocket. The company also told Ars Technica it aims to reach a weekly Starship launch cadence by early 2027 — an extraordinary tempo for the largest rocket ever flown, and the rate Musk says is needed to make Mars missions and a lunar presence feasible.

The catch attempt is the headline risk: snagging the Super Heavy booster out of the air with the launch tower's chopstick arms is the linchpin of rapid reuse. SpaceX says it has had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, suggesting the regulatory path for higher flight rates is clearing. If the catch works and cadence actually ramps, Starship stops being an experiment and starts being infrastructure.

Sources

  • Ars Technica: SpaceX to attempt Starship catch on next flight, with eye on rapid cadence increase

item.title: NASA rewrites how it picks science missions in "Faster to Science" overhaul
item.description:
NASA's Science Mission Directorate announced a major change to how it competes and selects science missions, arguing that the current process is too slow to deliver results at the pace the science community — and the moment — demands. The Faster to Science initiative reworks the competition and selection pipeline, and NASA will host a virtual Science Town Hall on Monday, October 26 to lay out the details.

This is a bureaucratic change with real consequences: mission selection mechanics determine which planetary, Earth science, and astrophysics missions fly, and when. Faster, more responsive selection could get instruments to targets years sooner, but the community will be watching closely to see whether speed comes at the cost of rigor. The town hall is the place to hear the specifics.

Sources

  • NASA: Faster to Science: A Letter to the Science Community

item.title: Perseverance sets the record for longest drive on another world: 45.22 km
item.description:
On Sol 2006 (October 11, 2026), NASA's Perseverance rover hit an odometer reading of 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles) — a new record for the farthest distance ever driven on another celestial body. Chief Engineer Vandi Verma recounts the milestone in a JPL blog post, noting the rover keeps rolling through Jezero Crater's terrain well into its extended mission.

The record is more than a bragging right. Every kilometer of driving validates autonomous navigation, mobility systems, and mission planning techniques that future sample-return and human missions will depend on. Perseverance is still collecting samples and exploring, and at this pace the record won't stand still for long — it'll keep extending itself.

Sources

  • NASA: Tracks Along the Longest Drive on Another World

item.title: SpaceX plans a Tesla merger and a first-ever full Starship catch next month
item.description:
Elon Musk said Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees of independent directors to explore a possible merger, formed at shareholders’ request. Musk called combining the companies an idea with “a lot of merit,” though he offered no names, terms, or timeline. The move would fold the world’s most valuable automaker and the world’s dominant launch provider into a single entity under one CEO.

Meanwhile, SpaceX will attempt next month to catch both Starship and its Super Heavy booster — the first time anyone has tried to recover an entire orbital launch vehicle. Full reusability has been the Starship program’s goal from the start; pulling it off would cut launch costs by an order of magnitude and mark a genuine milestone in the history of spaceflight.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Merging SpaceX and Tesla would be a "good idea," Musk says
  • The Verge: SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says

item.title: Japan launches MMX mission to bring back a piece of the Martian moon Phobos
item.description:
Japan has launched its MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission on a years-long journey to Phobos, the larger of Mars’s two moons. The mission’s climax comes in 2029, when the spacecraft will attempt up to two landings on Phobos’s surface to collect samples and bring them back to Earth.

A Phobos sample would be a scientific first and could help settle the debate over the moon’s origin — captured asteroid or debris from a giant impact on Mars — which in turn tells us about the early history of the inner solar system. MMX also keeps Japan’s steady rise in deep-space exploration on track, as sample-return missions become the country’s signature capability.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Japan launches mission to bring home a piece of the Martian moon Phobos

item.title: NASA updates progress on the rovers that will build its Moon Base
item.description:
NASA gave a progress update on the crewed and robotic rovers meant to support its Moon Base plans, where mobility systems will handle everything from astronaut transport and terrain mapping to scientific investigations and resource prospecting during early development. Data from these early missions will inform the infrastructure needed for astronauts to live and work on the Moon long-term.

Rovers are the unglamorous backbone of the lunar return: without reliable surface mobility, science and construction stay tethered to the lander. The update is another signal that NASA’s Moon Base effort is moving from architecture charts into hardware — the part of a space program where ambition gets tested against engineering reality.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Provides Progress Update on Moon Base Rovers

item.title: NASA’s SR-1 Freedom nuclear reactor advances toward deep-space flight
item.description:
NASA reported progress on the nuclear power module of SR-1 Freedom, the Space Reactor-1 mission announced at the agency’s “Ignition” event. SR-1 is designed to be humanity’s first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth’s orbit, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space, and NASA is moving quickly to develop the spacecraft.

Nuclear electric propulsion is one of the technologies that could make Mars-and-beyond missions practical: a fission reactor provides steady power for both propulsion and onboard systems over years of flight, far beyond what solar arrays can do in the outer solar system. The module’s progress is an early but real step toward opening the deep solar system to crewed missions.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA’s SR-1 Freedom Advances with Progress on Nuclear Power Module

item.title: NASA is redesigning Mars helicopter blades for longer, higher flights
item.description:
NASA researchers are developing the next generation of Mars helicopters, using high-fidelity computer simulations and wind tunnel tests to redesign rotorcraft blades that could fly higher and farther while doing science on the Red Planet. Ingenuity’s 72 flights proved powered flight works in Mars’s thin atmosphere; the new work aims to turn that proof of concept into a real exploration capability.

Aerial scouts change what rovers can do: a helicopter that flies farther can map terrain, scout routes, and carry instruments to places wheels can’t reach. The blade redesigns are the kind of unsexy engineering that quietly unlocks the next decade of Mars science.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Experimental Mars Helicopter Blade Designs Target Longer Flights

item.title: Webb unveils hidden stars and stellar jets in the NGC 7129 nursery
item.description:
NASA released a James Webb Space Telescope image of NGC 7129, a stellar nursery about 3,300 light-years from Earth, revealing a “cauldron of cosmic creation”: numerous stars previously hidden by dust clouds, lit up by Webb’s infrared vision, with jets streaming from young stars.

The image is a reminder of what Webb does best — turning familiar dark clouds into vivid star factories. Beyond the beauty shot, stellar jets are key to understanding how young stars shed angular momentum and how planet-forming disks evolve, so every detailed look at a nursery like this feeds directly into models of how solar systems are born.

Sources

  • NASA: Webb Captures Stellar Jets

item.title: Uzbekistan becomes the 77th Artemis Accords signatory
item.description:
The Republic of Uzbekistan became the 77th signatory of the Artemis Accords during a ceremony in Samarkand, committing to principles of safe, transparent, and responsible civil space exploration. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson noted that Uzbekistan joins at a pivotal moment, with the administration directing NASA to build toward a sustained lunar presence.

Each new signatory is mostly symbolic on its own — Uzbekistan isn’t building landers — but the Accords’ steady growth matters as a diplomatic project: it’s the framework the US is using to define the norms of lunar exploration before rival programs do. Seventy-seven nations is a bloc, and the Moon’s rules are being written by whoever shows up.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA Welcomes Uzbekistan as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory

item.title: Russian military satellite shadows a Ukraine-linked radar satellite at extreme range
item.description:
Russia's Kosmos 2612 spacecraft spent the weekend stalking ICEYE-X36, a commercial synthetic-aperture radar satellite widely believed to supply imagery to Ukraine. Tracking firm LeoLabs said the Russian satellite executed a deliberate sequence of maneuvers between October 15 and 19, closing from hundreds of kilometers to about 3 kilometers by Friday, then shifting positions ahead of and behind the commercial satellite over the weekend.

Independent analysts put the closest pass in the early hours of October 18 at a few hundred meters or less, and one automated forecast claimed as little as 26 meters, though that figure is disputed. LeoLabs had high confidence the objects came within about 500 meters, occasionally so close its radars struggled to distinguish them. A departure burn on October 18 sent Kosmos 2612 drifting away. ICEYE declined to comment, but Ukraine's military has used its imagery since 2022. Analysts call this the most advanced uncooperative rendezvous-and-proximity operation ever observed — sophisticated enough to inspect, shadow, or potentially interfere with another spacecraft.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: Russian spacecraft maneuvers in "extreme proximity" to satellite used by Ukraine

item.title: Piece of a Chinese rocket lands in a Minnesota farmer's cornfield
item.description:
A farmer combining his cornfield in Scott Township, west-central Minnesota, discovered an 11-foot-diameter circular metal object lying among the corn stalks. The Stevens County Sheriff's Office confirmed the metallic structure as "presumably a space object" and is working with state and federal agencies to identify its owner and arrange removal.

Experts have traced the debris to the September 15 launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket built by China's LandSpace, which deployed 10 satellites from Jiuquan, then reignited its engine and fell short of a full orbit — a 75-to-80-minute flight that rained debris across the American Midwest. Social media posts at the time showed fiery streaks heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The incident is now part of a growing pattern of large, uncontrolled reentries reaching populated areas, and a reminder that as launch rates climb, so does the odds of hardware coming down where people live and farm.

Sources

  • Space - Ars Technica: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield

item.title: NASA's simulated Mars crew marks one year locked inside a habitat
item.description:
The four members of NASA's CHAPEA Mission 2 crew have spent 365 days living in a 1,700-square-foot 3D-printed habitat at Johnson Space Center in Houston, simulating life on Mars — growing crops, managing limited resources, conducting suited extravehicular activities, and communicating with families only by email with a Mars-like delay. Commander Ross Elder, medical officer Ellen Ellis, science officer Matthew Montgomery, and flight engineer James Spicer entered the habitat on October 19, 2025.

They will exit on October 31 to conclude the 378-day mission, followed by two weeks of medical and psychological debriefs. NASA says the data will shape how future crews handle year-long missions with up-to-45-minute communication delays, informing decisions about food, exercise, medical care, and crew autonomy — knowledge that translates directly from Mars analogs to Artemis and any future Moon base operations.

Sources

  • NASA: NASA’s Simulated Mars Crew Marks One Year Inside Habitat

item.title: Curiosity watches the clouds roll by on the Red Planet
item.description:
NASA's Curiosity rover is ringing in a new Mars year, measured from the vernal equinox at the start of the northern hemisphere spring. In its latest blog entry, atmospheric scientist Alex Innanen describes the rover team tracking seasons by solar longitude and watching water-ice clouds drift overhead — a quiet reminder that Mars, for all its barrenness, has weather.

The update pairs with a newly released panorama capturing dawn on Mars, the most detailed view yet of the distant wind-carved cliffs and elongated ridges known as yardangs near Curiosity's path. The rover is now in its 14th Earth year on the surface and continues to return science from Gale Crater, studying ancient terrain that holds clues to Mars's wetter past.

Sources

  • NASA: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5036-5042: Watching the Clouds Go By
  • NASA: Martian Dawn
